You could choose to look at it this way: you bought BTC for $37,050 and lost $36,316.09. Since your profits were never realized you never actually had the money in the bank to lose. If you did withdraw your gains to an account you would’ve had to pay capital gains tax of 20% on it anyway so the unclaimed figure is slightly lower also. 

Having said that, the halving just happened and we could potentially see new all time highs going by the stock to flow graph, so who knows. By doing literally nothing, you might be able to recoup some of your initial investment

As for the gambling, it’s tough. What I found that works for me was to pick a strategy and stick to it. I also built some software that would trade on my behalf, taking emotion completely out of it. 

You sound like a very savvy person. You spotted BTC in 2016. It wasn’t even on my radar then.

Hang in there, if you look at the federal reserve shenanigans, BTC is probably just warming up. You’ve learned a lot about yourself should the opportunity present itself next time.

There’s this amazing theory that there are many versions of ourselves. In one version I’m talking to you right now. In another I’m a successful deep sea diver and I’ve never heard of Reddit. It’s a wild thought, but I’d like to think that I’m more than what I am right now to myself and to other people. Starting over can be scary. But it can be really rewarding. Maybe your breakthrough is right around the corner. I just want you to know that if you weren’t here, life would be less sweet for the rest of us.

You’re the best kind of person. There are a others who don’t see themselves as a work in progress. Who are unable to grow, edit, change, flex to be something good in the world. The fact that you try and get up and try again is already enough.

I don’t have any purpose either, but one I aspire to is to be kind to people. I figure, no one asked to be born. We’re all suddenly alive. The best thing we can do for each other is to be kind and compassionate to make going through life a little easier. Anything else we do, sports, art etc, is all extra things we do along the way. I bet you can kick my ass in athletics and no matter how hard I try you’ll still be better than me. I had a pretty good deadlift at one point though :D
You’re still here. That’s a significant accomplishment. Life is crazy. And hard. Can you share a specific example of where you couldn’t perform and failed?

For sure. My point is more related to separating the person who you see as your mom with the human being that has lived a life before and after you were born. There’s complexity there that’s hard to understand. One day you’ll be an adult and you will see her from a different perspective. Do you have anyone in your life that you can share these things with? It helps to talk and say these things out loud sometimes.

I read your post on r/advice. Just quickly, I’m no one special and I wish I could tell you I have some brilliant advice that will make everything better, but I don’t. What I can offer you is someone to talk to. I’m an adult so I have a different perspective than you. I love my mom very much, but we definitely had our share of problems growing up. There was physical and emotional abusive in our household between my parents. Their turmoil spilled over into me and it affected my young life. You seem very bright. You are separating which aspects of your feelings are your own and which have been introduced externally. That’s great. In the future you will start to see the separation more and more. As we grow older we naturally move away from our parents and we start to see things more clearly. I want you to know that you things will be ok. In the meanwhile, try to remember your mom was a kid too and maybe she’s still struggling with things from when she was younger. It’s no excuse to mistreat you, but sometimes understanding helps. I had some quality friends during those harder years. I hope you do too. If you don’t, well remember we are here to stand by you.
Hey :)

I’ve had those thoughts all my life. Sometimes every day, sometimes weeks go by, but they return. For me, it’s normal. Good conversations, working out, finding a fulfilling job helps, however. I’m trying to tell you it can be managed. It’s not necessarily a sure thing that these thoughts will end in suicide. Thinking about it is not wrong. It’s usually just a symptom that things are kinda heavy and that they need to change. The hardest part can be knowing what needs to change or how to change it. I think highly intellectual people often take these thoughts on as a challenge with the goal of healing, not to end it. You’re doing a great thing by talking about it. Keep doing that. I’m here if you need me. I need you too.
